name: Darjeeling
tagline: The thunderbolt town of tea, toy trains and Tenzing
meta_description: Darjeeling on a budget: the 1835 grant, Campbell's tea, HMI and Tenzing, the toy train, shared jeep fares, budget hotels, hostel beds and best months.
summary: Darjeeling is the hill town at about 2,042 m that grew from a Sikkimese ridge into a British sanatorium after 1835. Come for Kanchenjunga from Chowrasta, the toy train, HMI and the zoo, the tea slopes below town and Tibetan and Nepali food. Budget rooms cost ₹1,500–3,000; shared jeeps from Siliguri ₹250–350.

local_story.title: Dorje-ling, the thunderbolt place that became a town
paras: The name is usually traced to Tibetan: dorje, the thunderbolt sceptre of Buddhist ritual, and ling, a place. Tradition links it to a shrine called Dorje-ling on Observatory Hill, the wooded knoll above Chowrasta where the Mahakal temple now stands, and where Hindu and Buddhist priests still share the altar under the same prayer flags. The local account says the Bhutia Busty monastery first stood on this hill and moved downhill after damage in the Gorkha wars of the early 1800s. In 1828 two Company officers, Captain George Lloyd and J. W. Grant, passed what they called the 'Old Goorkha station called Dorjeling' and recommended it as a sanatorium.

On 1 February 1835 the Chogyal of Sikkim, Tsugphud Namgyal, signed a deed of grant handing the hill tract to the East India Company for a sanatorium, and was later paid an annual allowance for it. Dr Archibald Campbell of the Indian Medical Service became superintendent in 1839 and, around 1841, planted China tea seeds in his garden at Beechwood. They grew. By 1852 commercial gardens were being laid out at Tukvar, Steinthal and Aloobari, and today about 87 gardens make the tea that became India's first Geographical Indication product in 2004. The Lloyd family gave land for a botanic garden in 1878, and the railway arrived in 1881.

The town also became a place people came to rest, and sometimes to die. Sister Nivedita, the Irish-born disciple of Swami Vivekananda, died at Roy Villa on 13 October 1911; her memorial stands at the cremation ground below the railway station. Deshbandhu Chittaranjan Das died at his house, Step Aside, on 16 June 1925. Tenzing Norgay, who had come to Darjeeling as a young man and worked as a porter, made it his home after the 1953 Everest climb, and the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute opened here in 1954. In October 1959, months after the Dalai Lama's flight, Tibetan refugees set up a self-help centre at Hill Side, where carpets are still woven by hand.

did_you_know: The deed handing Darjeeling to the East India Company was signed on 1 February 1835 by the Chogyal of Sikkim, Tsugphud Namgyal, who was later paid an annual allowance for it.
Tenzing Norgay was the first Director of Field Training at the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute, founded on 4 November 1954, and was cremated on its grounds in 1986.
Two figures of the Bengal renaissance died in Darjeeling: Sister Nivedita at Roy Villa on 13 October 1911, and Deshbandhu C. R. Das at his house, Step Aside, on 16 June 1925.
intro: Darjeeling is a town of steep lanes on a ridge, and most of what visitors want sits within a 2 km walk of Chowrasta, the open square at the top. From there the Mall loops around Observatory Hill, Nehru Road drops past Glenary's and Keventer's, and on a clear October or March morning Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m and the third-highest mountain on Earth, fills the northern sky. Below the square the town gets denser and cheaper: Chowk Bazaar, the motor stand, the toy train station on Hill Cart Road and the Lloyd Botanic Garden.

We suggest three nights, and more if the weather is unsettled. Give one morning to the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute and the zoo, one to the tea slopes of Happy Valley and the Tibetan refugee centre on the Lebong road, and one to the toy train out to Batasia and Ghoom. Tiger Hill needs a 4 am start, so plan the rest of that day lightly. The town is easy on a budget: a hostel bed costs ₹400–700, a plate of momos ₹80–150, and almost everything is walkable, though the walking is uphill both ways.
facts: Tea, toy train, HMI, Kanchenjunga views
Jio, Airtel and BSNL good in town
costs: Shared jeep from NJP or Siliguri
Steam toy train joyride to Ghoom and back

highlights.title: Chowrasta and Observatory Hill
highlights.text: The flat square at the top of town, with the statue of Bhanubhakta Acharya (1814–1868), the poet who rendered the Ramayana into Nepali. A short climb behind it leads to the Mahakal shrine on Observatory Hill, where Hindu and Buddhist priests share one altar under prayer flags.

highlights.title: Himalayan Mountaineering Institute
highlights.text: Founded on 4 November 1954 after the first ascent of Everest. Its Everest Museum holds old boots, ice axes, oxygen sets and expedition photographs, and Tenzing Norgay, its first Director of Field Training, was cremated here in 1986. One ticket also covers the zoo next door.

highlights.title: Red pandas at the Himalayan zoo
highlights.text: The Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park opened in 1958 at about 2,100 m and runs breeding programmes for the red panda and the snow leopard. Go at opening time, when the animals are most active and the paths are quiet, and allow 90 minutes.

highlights.title: Happy Valley tea slopes
highlights.text: One of the older gardens, on Lebong Cart Road, a short walk below the town. Walk the plucking paths in the season from March to November and, when the factory is working, see withering and rolling. Visits depend on the day's work: check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre
highlights.text: Set up in October 1959 at Hill Side on the Lebong road by Tibetans who had followed the Dalai Lama into exile. Visitors can watch carpets being knotted on upright looms and buy rugs, woollens and small crafts directly from the centre's shop.

highlights.title: Lloyd Botanic Garden
highlights.text: A garden from 1878 on land given by the Lloyd family, terraced down the hill below Chowk Bazaar. Orchids, ferns, rhododendrons, old conifers, a glasshouse and very few people. A good, cheap hour when cloud hides the mountains.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps leave when full from the stands outside NJP station and along Hill Cart Road in Siliguri, through the morning and early afternoon. A seat costs ₹250–350 for the 65–70 km, about 3–3.5 hours via Kurseong or the Rohini road. Buy two seats if you want room for a bag.

The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway runs 88 km from NJP on 610 mm track, a slow full-day ride; first class costs roughly ₹1,400–1,700. Landslides and track work interrupt services, so book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel. Many people ride only the joyride from Darjeeling to Ghoom.

A small car from NJP or Bagdogra airport costs ₹3,000–4,000 and an SUV ₹3,500–5,000, about 3–3.5 hours. Use the prepaid counters or ask your hotel to send a driver. On a tight budget from Bagdogra, take a cab or auto to Siliguri and a shared jeep from there.

where_to_stay: For a budget base, stay between Chowrasta and Clubside: you walk everywhere and avoid the motor-stand noise. The Dekeling Hotel on Gandhi Road is a Tibetan family-run hotel 4–5 minutes below Chowrasta, and the state-run Meghbalika, the old Darjeeling Tourist Lodge, is on Bhanu Sarani a few minutes away. The GTA's Tenzing Norgay Youth Hostel on Dr Zakir Hussain Road, at the top of town, has a 44-bed dormitory and a few rooms for backpackers. The GTA also runs the Lowis Jubilee Complex on Dr S.K. Pal Road and the Maple Tourist Lodge in the Old Kutchery area. Rooms on Hill Cart Road near the station are cheaper but noisier.
tips: Book rooms early for Durga Puja, Diwali and the May–June school holidays, when much of Bengal heads uphill and prices rise.
Walk rather than drive inside the town: most sights are within 2 km of Chowrasta, and the one-way roads jam by mid-morning.
Carry a warm layer even in May; evenings drop to about 12 °C, and winter nights come close to freezing.
Book toy train joyrides on IRCTC as soon as your dates are fixed, and check current status before you travel.
If the mountains are hidden, wait: cloud often clears for an hour around dawn, so keep a second morning free.

experiences.title: HMI and the Himalayan zoo in one morning
experiences.summary: Walk about 2 km from Chowrasta to the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute, its Everest Museum and Tenzing Norgay's memorial, then see the red pandas and snow leopards of the Padmaja Naidu zoo on the same ticket. Best done at opening time, before the tour groups.
body: The Himalayan Mountaineering Institute was founded on 4 November 1954, a year after Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached the top of Everest. Tenzing, who had come to Darjeeling as a young man and worked as a porter on expeditions, became its first Director of Field Training and helped train a generation of Indian climbers here. When he died in 1986 he was cremated on the grounds, and his memorial and statue stand above the museum. The institute still runs mountaineering courses, so you may pass trainees in climbing boots on the road.

The Everest Museum is small and old-fashioned, and that is its charm: ice axes, boots, early oxygen sets, tents and faded expedition photographs, with labels that read like a climbing history lesson. Give it 45 minutes. The same ticket opens the Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park, opened in 1958 at about 2,100 m, which breeds red pandas and snow leopards for conservation. The red pandas are easiest to see in the morning, curled on branches or walking along the top of their enclosure.

Walk from Chowrasta: about 2 km and 30 minutes, with a climb at the end. Arrive at opening time, because tour cars come mid-morning and the zoo paths are crowded by 11 am. The zoo has a weekly closing day, which as we understand it is Thursday, and the ticket counter shuts in the afternoon, so check current status before you travel. Bring a jacket, as the hill is shaded and cold in winter, and keep the ticket with you for both gates.

faqs.q: Is one ticket valid for both HMI and the zoo?
faqs.a: Yes. As we understand it, a single joint ticket of roughly ₹100–150 for Indian visitors covers the Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park and the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute, including the Everest Museum. Foreign visitors pay more. Fees change from time to time, so check current status before you travel, and keep the ticket with you because it is checked at both gates.

faqs.q: How long do HMI and the zoo take?
faqs.a: Plan about three hours for both: 45 minutes to an hour in the Everest Museum and around Tenzing Norgay's memorial, and 90 minutes to two hours in the zoo. Add 30 minutes each way if you walk from Chowrasta. Starting at opening time gives you quieter paths and the best chance of seeing the red pandas moving.

faqs.q: Can I see snow leopards and red pandas there?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The Padmaja Naidu zoo runs breeding programmes for both and keeps them in large hillside enclosures. Red pandas are often asleep high in the trees by midday, so come early. Snow leopards are more active in cool weather. Sightings are never guaranteed, but patient morning visitors usually see at least one of the two.

experiences.title: Walk down to Happy Valley's tea slopes
experiences.cost: Free to walk · small fee for a factory tour
experiences.summary: A short walk below the town on Lebong Cart Road brings you into one of Darjeeling's older tea gardens. Walk the paths between the bushes, watch pluckers at work in season and, when the factory is running, see the leaf withered, rolled and dried.
body: Darjeeling's tea story began on these slopes. Dr Archibald Campbell, the superintendent, planted China seeds in his garden at Beechwood around 1841, and by 1852 the first commercial gardens were being laid out at Tukvar, Steinthal and Aloobari, all on the hills around the town. Happy Valley is one of the older gardens on this side, on Lebong Cart Road, and the easiest to reach for anyone without a car: you can walk there from the Chowk Bazaar area in about 30 minutes and walk back up for lunch.

From March to November pluckers work the rows, mostly women with baskets on their backs, taking two leaves and a bud. The first flush comes in March and April, light and flowery; the second flush in May and June is fuller, with the muscatel note that buyers pay most for. In the factory, when it is working, you can see the leaf spread in withering troughs, then rolled, oxidised and dried. The smell of the rolling room is the best part of the visit.

Visits are informal and depend on the day: some days the factory is not processing, and in winter the bushes are pruned and resting. Expect a small fee for a factory tour and a chance to buy tea at the garden. Wear shoes with grip, as the paths are steep and slippery after rain, and keep to the paths so you do not damage the bushes. Check current status before you travel, especially on Sundays and holidays.

faqs.q: Is Happy Valley Tea Estate open to visitors?
faqs.a: Yes, the garden takes visitors, and in the plucking season from March to November you can usually walk the paths and see the factory when it is working. Opening days and tour fees change, and the factory may be closed on some days and through the winter months. Check current status before you travel, ideally by asking your hotel the evening before.

faqs.q: How do I get to Happy Valley from the town?
faqs.a: Walk. The garden is on Lebong Cart Road, a short walk below the town: about 30 minutes down from the Chowk Bazaar area and a steeper 40 minutes back up. A taxi from the motor stand is the easy return if you would rather not climb. Combine it with the Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre, on the same side of town.

faqs.q: When is the best season for a tea garden visit?
faqs.a: March and April for the first flush, when the bushes are bright green and the factories run hard, and May and June for the second flush. October and November bring the autumn flush and clear mountain views. December to February is the quiet season: bushes are pruned and factories mostly idle, so you see the slopes but not the processing.

experiences.title: Carpet looms at the Tibetan refugee centre
experiences.image_query: Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre Darjeeling
experiences.summary: Since October 1959 Tibetan refugees have woven carpets at Hill Side, on the slope below town towards Lebong. Watch weavers knot wool at upright looms, see the stages of carpet making, and buy rugs and woollens from the centre's own shop rather than a middleman.
body: In March 1959 the Dalai Lama left Lhasa for India, and thousands of Tibetans followed him over the passes. Darjeeling, with old trade links to Tibet and long-settled Tibetan and Sherpa families, was one of the places they came to. In October 1959 a group of refugees set up the Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre at Hill Side, on the slope below the town towards Lebong, to give people work, schooling and a roof. Carpet weaving, a skill many of them carried with them, became the centre's living.

The workshops are open to visitors on working days. Weavers sit at tall upright looms, knotting wool row by row from a paper pattern, beating each row down and trimming the pile. The designs are the traditional ones: dragons, lotus flowers, snow lions and geometric borders. In other rooms you may see wool being prepared and dyed. Ask before photographing a weaver; most are happy to be photographed at the loom, but remember that it is their workplace, not a show.

The shop sells carpets, woollen jackets, bags and small crafts. Prices are fixed and the money goes to the centre, so this is a better place to buy a Tibetan rug than a shop on the Mall. Walk down from Chowrasta in about 40 minutes, or take a taxi from the motor stand. The centre usually closes on Sundays and on some Tibetan holidays, so check current status before you travel, and plan to take a taxi back up the hill.

faqs.q: Can visitors watch the weavers at work?
faqs.a: Yes. The weaving halls of the Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre are open to visitors on working days, free of charge, and you can stand beside the looms and watch carpets being knotted. Go in the morning, when most looms are busy, and ask before photographing anyone. The centre usually closes on Sundays and some holidays, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it a good place to buy a Tibetan carpet?
faqs.a: It is one of the most honest places to buy one. Prices are fixed and the money supports the centre rather than a dealer. A small rug costs a few thousand rupees and large carpets far more, depending on knot density and size. Ask whether shipping is possible for larger pieces, and what it costs, before you pay, and keep the receipt.

faqs.q: How far is the centre from Chowrasta?
faqs.a: Roughly 2–3 km downhill, about 40 minutes on foot through the lanes towards Lebong, and a stiff climb back. A taxi from the motor stand is the easy option for the return. Many people pair it with a walk to the Happy Valley tea garden, on the same side of town, and make a half day of the two.

experiences.title: Chowrasta to Observatory Hill on foot
experiences.summary: A slow morning loop around the top of town: Bhanubhakta's statue at Chowrasta, the shared Mahakal shrine on Observatory Hill where the name Dorje-ling began, the Mall with Kanchenjunga ahead, then breakfast at Keventer's or tea and cake at Glenary's.
body: Start at Chowrasta around 7 am, when the square belongs to early walkers, pony handlers and the first tea sellers. The statue at its centre is of Bhanubhakta Acharya (1814–1868), who rendered the Ramayana into Nepali and is honoured across the hills as the first poet of the language. On a clear morning walk to the north edge of the Mall: Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m, stands across the valleys, often pink for the first half hour after sunrise.

From the square, a short steep path climbs Observatory Hill to the Mahakal shrine. Tradition says a Buddhist shrine called Dorje-ling stood here, and that the town takes its name from it. Today Hindu and Buddhist priests serve side by side under thousands of prayer flags, a rare shared altar. Walk clockwise, follow what the people around you do with their shoes, and watch for the monkeys, which snatch offerings and spectacles. The local account also says the Bhutia Busty monastery first stood on this hill before it moved downhill.

Come down and walk the Mall loop round the hill, about 1.5 km and mostly level, then finish at Clubside, which takes its name from the Planters' Club. Have breakfast on the terrace at Keventer's, or tea and cake at Glenary's on Nehru Road; both are long-running town institutions and cost more than the lanes below, but they are worth one visit. The whole loop suits older walkers if taken slowly, with benches along the Mall.

faqs.q: Can anyone visit the Mahakal temple on Observatory Hill?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors of any faith are welcome at the Mahakal shrine, and entry is free. Dress modestly, walk clockwise around the shrines, follow the people around you on removing shoes, and ask before photographing worshippers or priests. Keep food and glasses out of sight, because the monkeys on the hill are bold and quick. Early morning is the quietest time.

faqs.q: Where can I see Kanchenjunga from Darjeeling town?
faqs.a: From the north side of Chowrasta and the Mall loop around Observatory Hill, on clear mornings. October to early December and March to April give the best odds. Be out by about 6–6:30 am, because cloud often rises from the valleys by 9 am. You do not need Tiger Hill to see the mountain, though Tiger Hill gives a wider view.

faqs.q: Is the walk suitable for older people?
faqs.a: Mostly, yes. The Mall loop around Observatory Hill is paved and fairly level, about 1.5 km, with benches along the way. The path up Observatory Hill itself is short but steep, roughly ten minutes of steps, so older walkers can take it slowly or skip it. Allow two hours with stops for tea and the view.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Darjeeling?
faqs.a: October to early December and March to May. October and November give the clearest Kanchenjunga views and dry, cool days; spring brings rhododendrons and the first flush in the tea gardens. Winter is cold, about 2–9 °C in January, but often clear. June to September is wet, with most of the year's 3,000 mm or so of rain, landslides and few views, but low prices.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Three nights is a good minimum. Use one morning for Tiger Hill and the toy train, one for HMI, the zoo and Observatory Hill, and one for Happy Valley and the Tibetan refugee centre. Add a fourth night if the weather is unsettled, for a second chance at a clear dawn, or add a night in Lamahatta or Lepchajagat for village quiet.

faqs.q: How do I get from NJP or Bagdogra to Darjeeling cheaply?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from the stand outside NJP station or from Hill Cart Road in Siliguri: ₹250–350 a seat, about 3–3.5 hours for 65–70 km. From Bagdogra airport, take a cab or auto to Siliguri first. A reserved small car costs ₹3,000–4,000 and an SUV ₹3,500–5,000, which is worth it for a family of four with luggage.

faqs.q: Can I take the toy train from NJP to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes, when the full-line service runs. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway covers 88 km from NJP on 610 mm track, a slow full-day ride; first class costs roughly ₹1,400–1,700. Landslides and track work interrupt services, so book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel. The joyride from Darjeeling to Ghoom is the easy alternative.

faqs.q: How much does a budget trip to Darjeeling cost per day?
faqs.a: Roughly ₹1,500–2,500 a person a day on a shoestring: a hostel bed at ₹400–700 or a shared budget room, momos and thalis at ₹100–250 a meal, and walking instead of taxis. A comfortable mid-range day, with a ₹2,500–3,000 double room, a toy train joyride and a share of a Tiger Hill car, comes to about ₹3,000–4,500 a person.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Darjeeling?
faqs.a: No. Indian and foreign visitors need no permit for Darjeeling town, Ghoom or Tiger Hill; foreigners carry their passport and visa, which hotels record at check-in. Permits apply when you go on into Sikkim, where foreigners need a Restricted Area Permit, and in protected areas such as Singalila National Park. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What should I pack for Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Layers in every season. In winter bring a down jacket, thermals, cap and gloves: January runs about 2–9 °C and many budget rooms are unheated. In spring and autumn a fleece and light jacket do for the day, with warmer clothes for dawn. In the monsoon pack a good umbrella, quick-dry clothes and shoes with grip for wet, steep lanes.

faqs.q: Where can I eat cheaply in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: In the small Tibetan and Nepali kitchens around the Chowk Bazaar, the motor stand and the lanes below Chowrasta: momos for ₹80–150 a plate, thukpa for ₹100–180 and a thali for ₹150–250. Tea rooms charge ₹40–150 a pot or cup of Darjeeling tea. Glenary's and Keventer's cost more but are worth one breakfast.

faqs.q: When is Darjeeling most crowded?
faqs.a: During the Durga Puja and Diwali holidays in October and November, at Christmas and New Year, and in the May–June school holidays, when traffic jams and room prices rise. Late October after the pujas, mid-November, March and early April are calmer and still often clear. Weekdays are quieter everywhere, including at Tiger Hill.
